q: How is a RICE score calculated?
options: Reach x Impact x Confidence / Effort
why: Higher reach, impact and confidence raise the score; more effort lowers it. It ranks value per unit of work.

q: A cost performance index (CPI) of 0.8 means:
options: You earn $0.80 of planned value for every $1 spent: over budget
You have spent 80% of the budget
why: CPI = earned value / actual cost. Below 1 means each dollar buys less than planned.

q: Under the 0/100 rule for earned value, an item earns its value:
options: In proportion to the days worked
why: It stops people claiming 90% done forever. Work counts when it is finished.

q: The expected monetary value (EMV) of a risk is:
why: A 20% chance of a $50,000 problem has an EMV of $10,000. Summing EMVs gives a starting point for a contingency reserve.

q: Little's Law relates average work in progress (WIP) to:
why: WIP = throughput x cycle time. To shorten cycle time without more throughput, limit work in progress.

options: Story points completed per sprint, used to forecast how much fits in the next one
why: Use the average of recent sprints, not the best one, so forecasts are honest.

q: Which is a well-written key result?
options: Reduce weekly report preparation time from 6 hours to 2
why: A key result is a measurable proof of the objective. 'Launch X' is a task, not a result.

q: Which backlog item title is best?
options: Add a date filter to the sales dashboard so users can view one month
why: A clear title says what changes and for whom, so anyone can pick it up and know when it is done.

q: What determines the earliest finish date of a project?
options: The longest chain of dependent tasks (the critical path)
why: The critical path is the longest sequence of dependent tasks. A delay on it delays the finish; tasks with float can slip without that effect.

q: After month 1, 40% of new users have not come back. What does this measure?
why: Retention is the share of users who return after a period. It shows whether people keep finding value.

q: What is the point of a retrospective?
options: To agree at least one concrete change for the next sprint, using the numbers
why: A retro that changes nothing wastes the time. Pick one change, and check it next time.

q: The five disciplines graphic is best described as...
options: A summary of common advice, inspired by HBS
why: It credits a third party and says only 'inspired by' HBS research.

q: Best way to use your lowest rating?
why: One concrete practice and a review date beats five resolutions.

q: You lengthen a task that has 3 days of float by 2 days. The project finish...
why: Float is the slip a task can absorb without delaying the finish; 2 days is inside 3.
